section.title: When Israel Went Out from Egypt
section.sectionRationale: The second psalm of the Egyptian Hallel, this compact hymn compresses the exodus and wilderness years into vivid poetic snapshots, personifying sea, river, mountains, and hills as trembling before the presence of the LORD who once split the waters and later split the rock.
section.thesis: The same LORD who made the sea flee and the Jordan turn back at Israel's exodus is the LORD before whom the whole earth must tremble now, the God who turns hard rock into flowing water for His thirsty people.
section.frameNote: Two matched movements: the exodus and creation's tiptoeing response, verses 1-4, and the psalmist's probing questions answered by a call for all the earth to tremble before the God who provides water from the rock, verses 5-8.

units.label: Judah became God's sanctuary
units.note: the exodus and creation on tiptoe

verses.text: When Israel departed from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of foreign tongue,
Judah became God's {{miqdash|sanctuary}}, Israel His dominion.
The sea observed and fled; the Jordan turned back;
the mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs.

units.label: Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord
units.note: probing questions, water from the rock

verses.text: Why was it, O sea, that you fled, O Jordan, that you turned back,
O mountains, that you skipped like rams, O hills, like lambs?
Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob,
who turned the rock into a pool, the {{challamish|flint}} into a fountain of water!

miqdash.gloss: Sanctuary, holy place. That Judah itself becomes God's dwelling place shows the exodus was never merely political rescue but the creation of a people among whom God would personally live.

challamish.gloss: Flint, a notably hard stone. That God turns the hardest, most unyielding rock into a fountain underscores that no obstacle, however impenetrable, resists His power to provide for His thirsty people.

basic.context: This brief hymn compresses roughly forty years of Israel's history, the crossing of the Red Sea, the giving of the law at Sinai, and the provision of water in the wilderness, into eight vivid lines, personifying sea, river, and mountains as fleeing and dancing before the presence of the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm's poetic device, addressing nature directly and asking why it trembled, is not mere literary flourish but a summons to the reader to recognize that the same overwhelming presence that once moved creation itself is present and active now, still worthy of trembling reverence.
basic.originalLanguages: Judah becomes God's miqdash, sanctuary, verse 2, the dwelling place of His presence among His people. And in the psalm's climactic image, God turns challamish, flint, an especially hard and unyielding stone, into a fountain of water, showing that no obstacle can resist His provision.
basic.typology: The rock that gives water in the wilderness, recalled in verse 8, is identified by Paul as a type of Christ, for they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and that Rock was Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4, the true and better source of living water for God's thirsty people.
basic.christ: Paul explicitly identifies the rock that gave Israel water in the wilderness as a type of Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4, so the flint turned to a fountain in this psalm anticipates Jesus, who offers living water welling up to eternal life, John 4:10-14, and who cried out at the feast, If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink, John 7:37-39. Luke describes Jesus' own coming departure as an exodus, Luke 9:31, linking His death and resurrection directly to the deliverance this psalm celebrates.
basic.god: God's mere presence is so overwhelming that seas flee and mountains leap like startled lambs; He personally makes His dwelling among His redeemed people and provides abundantly for them even from the hardest, most unpromising sources.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 14:21-22 records the parting of the Red Sea recalled in verse 3. Joshua 3:14-17 records the Jordan's parting for the second, later generation. 1 Corinthians 10:4 identifies the rock of verse 8 as a type of Christ, the true source of living water.
basic.oneStory: The LORD whose presence made the sea flee and the rock pour water at the exodus is the same LORD whose presence the whole earth must tremble before, and the rock that gave Israel water in the wilderness points forward to Christ, the true Rock, who gives living water to everyone who is thirsty and leads His people through a greater exodus, from death into life.

context.literary:
The psalm is two stanzas of four lines, and the second answers the first the way a teacher's question answers a puzzle. Verses 1 to 4 state what happened: a long temporal clause opens the poem, 'When Israel departed from Egypt,' and its main clause is held back until verse 2, so the first thing the ear receives is the going out itself. Verses 5 to 8 turn and question the very things just named, in the same order, sea and Jordan, then mountains and hills, and then give one answer that is wider than the question, 'Tremble, O earth.'

The most striking device is withheld speech. In verses 1 to 6 God is never named. The sanctuary and dominion of verse 2 carry only a pronoun, 'His,' and the sea and the mountains react to a cause the poem has not yet shown. Only in verse 7 does the title arrive, 'the Lord,' then 'the God of Jacob,' and with it the reason for everything. The effect is of a hush before an unveiling.

There is also a frame. 'The house of Jacob' stands in verse 1 and 'the God of Jacob' in verse 7, so the people and their God are bound by one name around the whole poem. Inside that frame the pairs run in parallel: sea against Jordan, mountains against hills, rams against lambs, rock against flint, pool against fountain. Nothing is dull repetition; each pair widens the picture from the great to the small.

The order of events is not chronological. The sea comes first, the Jordan second, Sinai's quaking third and the rock last, though the rock at Horeb came before the Jordan by forty years. The poet arranges by theme and sound rather than calendar, so that the two crossings stand together as the first and last waters of the journey and the whole wilderness lies compressed between them.
context.historical:
The psalm is undated and unattributed in the Hebrew, and it should not be pinned to a particular king or crisis. What can be said is how it was used. It sits in the Egyptian Hallel, Psalms 113 to 118, and the Mishnah's description of the Passover meal assumes that these psalms are sung over its cups, with a famous line that every generation must see itself as having come out of Egypt. Exodus had already told parents to give their children an answer when they asked about the meaning of the service, Exodus 12:26-27, and this poem is that answer set to music.

Three events lie behind the lines. The sea is the crossing of Exodus 14, when the Egyptians themselves cried, 'Let us flee from the Israelites,' Exodus 14:25, a flight that the psalm hands over to the water. The Jordan is Joshua 3, and the detail worth noticing is the season. The river was overflowing its banks at harvest, Joshua 3:15, so the stopping of the current was a feat at its most difficult. The mountains recall Sinai, where the earth trembled before the God of Israel, Judges 5:4-5 and Psalm 68:7-8. The water from the rock belongs to two episodes, Exodus 17:6 at Horeb and Numbers 20:11 at Kadesh near the end of the forty years.

'A people of foreign tongue' sounds as though it was spoken by someone who remembered what it was like to be surrounded by an unintelligible language. Psalm 81:5 uses the same memory of hearing a language not understood in Egypt.

Many scholars have also observed that a sea and a river appear together as paired rivals in the myths of Canaan's neighbours. Israel's poets knew those pictures and borrowed their shape, but they tell a different story: no rival god is fought here, and the water simply yields to the Lord of Israel's history.
context.canonical:
Psalm 114 is a small anthology of earlier texts. The song of Moses after the sea had already said that the nations would hear and tremble, Exodus 15:14, and that the Lord would plant His people on the mountain of His inheritance, in the sanctuary His hands had established, Exodus 15:17. Psalm 114:2 gives that sanctuary a different meaning: the sanctuary is not a place on the mountain but a people. The Jordan is told in Joshua 4:23-24 to be remembered just as the Red Sea was, so that all the peoples of the earth might know the Lord's hand.

Other psalms and prophets return to the same waters when they need hope. Psalm 66:6 says the sea became dry land and 'there we rejoiced in Him.' Psalm 77:16 describes the waters seeing God and being shaken. Isaiah 51:9-10 pleads that the arm that once dried the sea would act again, and Isaiah 43:16-19 promises a new way through the waters for a new exodus. Water from stone becomes a pattern for promised renewal in Psalm 107:35 and Isaiah 41:18, where the desert itself turns into a pool.

The Septuagint counts Psalms 114 and 115 together as a single psalm, which is why numbering in some Bibles runs one behind the Hebrew for this stretch of the Psalter.

In the New Testament, Paul makes the strongest use. He tells the Corinthians that the fathers were baptised in the cloud and in the sea and drank from the spiritual rock, and that these things happened as examples and were written down for us, 1 Corinthians 10:1-4 and 10:11. Luke's account of the transfiguration says Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about the exodus He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31, and Hebrews 12:26 recalls the voice that shook the earth and promises a further shaking.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet wanted worshippers to feel the exodus as something still happening to the whole world, not as a museum piece. By holding God's name back until verse 7 he makes the audience wait inside the story, watching waters run backward and hills jump, and only then does he tell them who stood behind it. The intended effect is reverence, not curiosity.

The mocking tone of verses 5 and 6 is deliberate. The poet turns on the sea and the mountains and asks them what ailed them, as one might tease a bully who has just been humbled. The sea that had frightened sailors, the river that had stood in front of an army, the mountains that seemed immovable, all hurried out of the way. The first hearers were meant to conclude that if the greatest powers they knew had fled, there was no force left for Israel to fear.

He also meant them to receive the final image personally. Water from flint was not only history but Israel's daily need: a dry country, a precarious harvest, a people who were always one drought from the wilderness. The psalm tells them that the Lord who did that is the one who is still turning stone to spring.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes what the Lord did at the sea, the Jordan, Sinai and the rock. It gives only one command, 'Tremble, O earth,' and that command is about posture, not about technique. A reader should not infer that every blocked road will open or that every drought will end on cue, since Israel's story itself includes seasons in which the water did not come, and the generation that saw the sea still died in the wilderness, 1 Corinthians 10:5.

The psalm also keeps the miracle narrow in its language. It does not say that Israel earned the rescue, and it does not say the rock yielded because Moses struck it well. Numbers 20:10-12 records that Moses' own handling of the second rock was faulty, yet the water still came, which shows that the provision rested on God's character, not on the performer's merit.

What carries forward is a way of seeing. A believer facing a closed sea or a hard stone is invited to remember the One who is named in verse 7, and to take the posture of trembling reverence that the poem prescribes, not as dread but as fitting respect for a Lord who has proved Himself in ways that cannot be explained by nature alone.

debates.question: Is the sea, Jordan, mountains and hills language mere poetry, or does it make a larger claim?

views.label: A literary device for a real, historical rescue
views.case: Hebrew poetry personifies nature freely. Psalm 97:4 says the earth 'sees and trembles,' and Psalm 29:6 has Lebanon skip like a calf. In this reading the poet is using the ordinary vocabulary of awe to describe two river crossings and one quaking mountain, with no more claim to sentient hills than we make when we say a storm was angry.

views.label: A deliberate answer to the myths of the neighbours
views.case: Because sea and river appear as paired powers in the stories of Canaan's neighbours, the poem can be read as a pointed reply. The waters that other nations feared as gods are here only obedient creatures that run when the true Lord appears. On this view the personification is polemic: it strips the powers of their rank without needing any belief that water has a will.

views.label: A glimpse of creation's real responsiveness
views.case: Scripture elsewhere pictures creation as answering its Maker, Romans 8:22, and Jesus rebuking a storm that obeys, Mark 4:41. The psalm may be speaking of a true if mysterious creaturely response to God's presence, not decoration.

debates.bearing: All three readings land the same point. Nothing in the created order, however vast or frightening, stands between God and what He has promised, and that is exactly why the psalm calls the whole earth, not only the waters, to tremble.

debates.question: What does 'Judah became God's sanctuary' refer to?

views.label: The wilderness camp and the tabernacle
views.case: Judah marched first on the east side, Numbers 2:3, so the tribe that led the people into the land could stand for the whole people. On this view the verse describes the moment at Sinai when God took up residence in the midst of the camp and Israel became His realm.

views.label: Zion and the temple in Judah's territory
views.case: Psalm 78:68-69 says God chose the tribe of Judah and Mount Zion and built His sanctuary there. Read this way, verse 2 telescopes the exodus toward its goal, a house in Jerusalem, and the poem was sung by pilgrims who lived in that fulfilment.

views.label: The whole redeemed people, wherever they are
views.case: Because the verse says the people themselves became the sanctuary and dominion, some read it as stating a principle: God's dwelling is wherever He has redeemed a people. This fits the later claim that believers are God's temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16.

debates.bearing: The first two views anchor the line in Israel's history, and the third explains why the New Testament can reuse it. All three agree that the exodus aimed at a presence more than at a place.

study.originalLanguages:
The command in verse 7, 'Tremble,' comes from a root that is used for the pangs of childbirth. The same root gives the 'anguish' that seizes the people of Philistia when they hear of the exodus, Exodus 15:14, and it is the verb for God's giving birth to Israel in Deuteronomy 32:18, 'the God who gave you birth.' To tremble before the Lord in this psalm is therefore more than shivering; it is to writhe in the pains of something being born. The word is addressed to the earth, and the Hebrew word for earth is feminine, so the imperative is a feminine form.

The verbs of retreat in verse 3 carry military overtones. The word for 'fled' is the word the Egyptians used when they said 'Let us flee from the Israelites,' Exodus 14:25, and Psalm 104:7 uses it for the waters hurrying away at God's rebuke. The psalm lets the sea do what Pharaoh's army did. The verb for 'skipped' in verses 4 and 6 is the verb of dancing in Ecclesiastes 3:4, 'a time to dance,' and of Lebanon leaping like a calf in Psalm 29:6. Hebrew calls the lambs 'sons of the flock,' so the hills are pictured as young animals, small and startled.

The last verse is built on a participle, 'the one turning,' with a definite article. It does not say the Lord turned the rock once; it names Him by what He habitually does, the Turner of rock. 'Rock' here is the common word tsur, which is also a title for God, Deuteronomy 32:4. The same verse that praises His works in the wilderness calls Him by the name of the thing He transformed. The 'pool' of verse 8 is a word the prophets reuse for the renewal of the desert, Isaiah 41:18 and Isaiah 35:7, so the psalm's last image already looks beyond Sinai.

The titles in verse 7 are chosen with care. 'Lord' is the word adon, a title of lordship, not the covenant name, and 'God' is the poetic singular Eloah. Together with 'of Jacob' they give the hearer a majestic title and then a very personal one: the ruler of the earth is the God of that patriarch whose name Israel bears. The people are called 'the house of Jacob' in verse 1, so name and God meet at the two ends of the psalm.

'Sanctuary' in verse 2 is the word used in the song at the sea for the place His hands established, Exodus 15:17. 'Dominion' is a plural form of a word for rule or realm, which makes Israel the territory over which He reigns.

typology.type: The rock that gave water, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: The water-giving rock was struck at Horeb, Exodus 17:6, and Paul says the spiritual rock that accompanied Israel 'was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. The escalation lies in who is struck: at Calvary a soldier's spear brought out blood and water, John 19:34, and Jesus invited the thirsty to come to Him and drink, John 7:37-39. The type has a limit, since the original rock supplied one wandering nation's thirst for a season, while the water Christ gives becomes a spring in the one who drinks, John 4:14.

typology.type: The sea and the Jordan, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: Both waters were crossed by God's people on dry ground, the first leaving slavery and the second entering rest. Paul reads the sea as a kind of baptism into Moses, 1 Corinthians 10:2, and in Christ believers are baptised into His death and walk in newness of life, Romans 6:3-4. The correspondence escalates because the baptism is into a person who actually passed through death, not a mere river. It stays partial, for the first generation passed through water and still fell in the wilderness, 1 Corinthians 10:5, whereas those united to Christ share His risen life.

typology.type: Judah as the Lord's sanctuary, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: The tribe from which David and later the Messiah would come is called His holy place. In Christ the temple language reaches its fullest sense: Jesus spoke of the temple of His body, John 2:19-21, and His people, built together as living stones, become a dwelling for God in the Spirit, Ephesians 2:21-22 and 1 Peter 2:4-5. The type is surpassed because a place in Judah could be destroyed, while the living temple is raised again and finally needs no building, since the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22.

typology.type: Water from flint as the pattern of the new exodus, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: The prophets took water in the desert as a sign of the coming renewal, Isaiah 41:18 and Isaiah 44:3, where the Lord promises to pour water on thirsty ground and His Spirit on the offspring. John explains that the streams of living water Jesus speaks of mean the Spirit, John 7:39. The shape finally appears as a river flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1. The type falls short only in scale, since Israel's pool lasted a camping season and the river of life never dries.

study.christ:
The psalm does not name a Messiah, and it is best to say so before seeing Him in it. The New Testament reads it in three ways, each tied to a text, and each deserves to be held lightly where the text stops speaking.

First, by identity. Paul says the rock that accompanied Israel was Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4. This is not a clever allegory of a boulder. It rests on the Old Testament's own habit of calling God 'the Rock,' Deuteronomy 32:4 and Psalm 18:2, together with the New Testament's conviction that the Son was present and active in Israel's history. The one who turned the flint into a fountain is the one who later stood up in the temple at the feast and said that if anyone is thirsty he should come and drink, John 7:37-39. In saying this He was not merely borrowing a metaphor; He was claiming the role the psalm gives to the Lord.

Second, by pattern. Luke says Moses and Elijah talked with Jesus on the mountain about the 'departure' He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31. The Greek word is exodos. Jesus' death and rising are not merely like the exodus; they are the exodus to which the first one pointed, a deliverance from a harder bondage through a deeper water. Isaiah 51:9-10 had already asked the arm of the Lord to do again what He did at the sea, and the gospel announces that He has.

Third, by the sanctuary. In verse 2 the people become God's dwelling. Jesus identifies the temple with His own body, John 2:19-21, and the church is built on the cornerstone Isaiah promised, Isaiah 28:16 and Ephesians 2:21-22. Wherever the Lord's presence is, there the earth is told to tremble, and the same writer who calls Him a consuming fire urges worship with reverence and awe, Hebrews 12:28-29.

Where to stop. The psalm gives no basis for turning every detail into a code. The ram-like mountains and the Jordan are not secret portraits of Jesus. The honest link is that the God of verse 8 is the God who in Christ provides life from what looks like death, and that this exodus pattern is carried by the New Testament's own words. The thirst is real, the supply is real, and the Rock who supplies has a name.
study.god:
The psalm gives a doctrine of God by showing how creation behaves in His presence. The sea runs, the river reverses, the mountains leap, the earth shakes. None of this is a display of anger. The poem never says God was furious; it says the world could not stay still. His presence has a weight that matter itself must answer, and that is a very high view of what it means for God to be near.

That nearness is also commanded of the whole earth, not only Israel. Verse 7 turns from the people to the globe, as Psalm 96:9 does when it says to tremble before Him, all the earth, and Psalm 99:1 when it says the nations should tremble. The God who made a covenant with a single family is Lord of every landscape. The particular and the universal sit in the same sentence, 'the God of Jacob' and 'the earth.'

He is both tremendous and tender, and the psalm will not let either go. The same Lord who makes the mountains jump is the one who brings a drink out of flint for a complaining people, Exodus 17:3. He does not scold the thirst; He meets it. Power and provision are held in one participle, 'who turns,' as if turning rock into a pool were simply the kind of thing He does.

He is faithful to a people who often failed Him. Verse 2 says Israel became His own realm, and that line comes from a nation that had grumbled at the sea, complained at the rock and refused the land. The psalm shows God rescuing without waiting for good behaviour, for He chose them in their slavery.

He is sovereign over the powers that other nations feared. Water, river and mountain are not rivals. They are creatures, and when the Creator appears they step aside. That is the same truth Joshua told the people, that the Jordan was dried so that all the peoples of the earth would know the hand of the Lord, Joshua 4:23-24.

For worship, the psalm teaches that the right response to such a God is neither mere cheer nor mere fear but trembling that makes room. It also gives a reason to hope in drought, since the God who is praised here is the one named as a Turner of stone into spring.

crossReferences.note: The song at the sea looks ahead to the very things the psalm celebrates. The people tremble, the Lord leads them in loving devotion to His holy dwelling, and He plants them in the sanctuary His hands established. Psalm 114:2 is a reading of that promise: the sanctuary is made of people, and Judah and Israel are what God's hands built.

The crossing behind verse 3. The waters stand as a wall, the Egyptians flounder and finally say 'Let us flee.' The psalm takes their word of retreat and gives it to the sea itself, so that the army and the water do the same thing in the presence of the same Lord.

The Jordan crossing, in flood at harvest. The stopping of the current began when the priests carrying the ark touched the water, so the psalm's line that the Jordan turned back is tied to the presence of God's ark in the river, not to some natural change.

Joshua explains why the Jordan was dried, comparing it to the Red Sea, 'so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty.' The psalm's wide call to the earth to tremble in verse 7 is this purpose spoken aloud.

Deborah's song describes the mountains quaking before the LORD, the One of Sinai, the God of Israel. It is the clearest earlier source for the skipping hills of verses 4 and 6, and shows that the trembling mountains belonged to Israel's old memory of Sinai.

A voice of the LORD makes Lebanon skip like a calf. The same picture of mountains behaving like frisky young animals appears in another psalm in the setting of a storm, which shows the image was a stock way of speaking of God's power over the land.

Asaph's retelling of the wilderness says God split the rocks and gave drink as abundant as the seas, bringing streams from stone. It confirms that the water from the rock was a heritage Israel taught to every generation, and that verse 8 belongs to a larger catechism.

God promises to turn the desert into a pool of water and the dry land into flowing springs. The prophet takes the psalm's own images of pool and spring and sets them in the future, so the exodus becomes the pattern for what God will do again for His people.

Paul reads the cloud, the sea, the food and the drink as things that happened to the fathers, then adds that they drank from the spiritual rock and that the rock was Christ. He uses the wilderness story as a mirror for the Corinthians, warning that privilege is no guarantee of survival.

At the Feast of Booths, which recalled the wilderness and included a ceremony of water, Jesus invites the thirsty to Himself and promises streams of living water. John's own comment that He meant the Spirit identifies the new gift as the true fulfilment of the spring from flint.

Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about the departure He will accomplish in Jerusalem. The word for departure is exodus, and Luke thereby names the cross and resurrection as the exodus that the sea and Jordan foreshadowed.

The writer recalls the voice that shook the earth at Sinai, promises a final shaking, and calls believers to worship with reverence and awe because they receive an unshakable kingdom. The psalm's call to tremble becomes a call to hold on to what cannot be shaken.

study.oneStory:
The psalm sits where creation and redemption touch. In Genesis 1 God divides the waters and sets the land in place, and in the flood the waters are lifted up again as a threat. The exodus is the Lord once more mastering the waters, but this time for the sake of a people, and the psalm celebrates that the water now serves what God is doing in history. The sea that once covered the earth now makes a road.

The story goes forward from here with a hard edge. The generation that crossed the sea did not enter the land; their children crossed the Jordan, and the psalm names both waters because they hold the whole span of the wilderness between. Yet the exodus did not end the need for it. Israel went into exile and prayed that the arm of the Lord would wake and do again what it had done at the sea, Isaiah 51:9-10. The prophets promised a new exodus in which rivers would open in the heights and a way would appear in the waters, Isaiah 41:18 and Isaiah 43:16-19.

That promise runs into Jesus. At the Jordan He is baptised, in the wilderness He is tested after forty days, and on the mountain He speaks with Moses about the exodus He will accomplish at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31. The water and the rock both become gifts of Him, John 7:37-39. His resurrection is the true crossing, and His people, baptised into His death, walk in newness of life, Romans 6:3-4.

The psalm's last theme, that the earth itself should tremble before the Lord, is also the Bible's final hope. The creation that fled at His presence will at the end be remade, and there will be a river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1. The thirsty are invited to drink freely from the spring of the water of life, Revelation 21:6. The God who turned flint into a fountain finishes by turning a cursed and thirsty world into one that is watered at its source, and His dwelling is with man, Revelation 21:3.

quiz.q: According to verse 2, what does Judah become when Israel departs from Egypt?

options.text: God's sanctuary, with Israel as His dominion.
options.note: The exodus was not merely political freedom but the creation of a people among whom God personally dwells.

options.text: An independent nation with no connection to God.
options.note: The verse explicitly names Judah as God's sanctuary, a place of His presence, not mere political independence.

options.text: A vassal state under Egyptian rule still.
options.note: The psalm celebrates departure from Egypt, the opposite of remaining a vassal state.

options.text: A temporary military outpost.
options.note: The term used, sanctuary, describes God's dwelling place, not merely a military installation.

quiz.q: What two bodies of water are personified as fleeing and turning back in verse 3?

options.text: The sea and the Jordan.
options.note: These recall the Red Sea crossing at the exodus and the Jordan crossing under Joshua.

options.text: The Nile and the Euphrates.
options.note: The text specifically names the sea and the Jordan, not the Nile or Euphrates.

options.text: The Dead Sea and the Sea of Galilee.
options.note: These particular bodies of water are not the ones named in the psalm's exodus imagery.

options.text: Only the Jordan, with no mention of the sea.
options.note: Both the sea and the Jordan are explicitly named together in verse 3.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist call all the earth to do in verse 7?

options.text: Tremble at the presence of the Lord, the God of Jacob.
options.note: This direct address extends the exodus narrative's implications to a universal summons to reverence.

options.text: Ignore what happened at the exodus as ancient history.
options.note: The verse commands active, reverent trembling, not indifference to God's past acts.

options.text: Rebuild the temple in Jerusalem immediately.
options.note: The command given is to tremble in reverence, not a specific building project.

options.text: Celebrate only once a year during Passover.
options.note: The command to tremble is not restricted to a single annual observance but is a standing summons.

quiz.q: What miraculous provision does verse 8 describe God performing?

options.text: Turning the rock into a pool, the flint into a fountain of water.
options.note: This recalls God's wilderness provision of water from the hardest stone, Exodus 17:6, Numbers 20:11.

options.text: Turning water into wine at a wedding feast.
options.note: That miracle belongs to Jesus' ministry in John 2, not this psalm's exodus and wilderness imagery.

options.text: Multiplying loaves and fishes for a crowd.
options.note: That is a Gospel miracle, not the wilderness rock imagery described in this psalm.

options.text: Causing manna to stop falling from heaven.
options.note: The psalm describes water flowing from rock, not the cessation of manna.

quiz.q: How does Paul apply the rock imagery of verse 8 in 1 Corinthians 10:4?

options.text: He identifies the rock that gave Israel water as a type of Christ Himself.
options.note: Paul explicitly states that Rock was Christ, connecting this psalm's imagery directly to Jesus as the source of living water.

options.text: He denies any connection between the rock and Christ.
options.note: Paul makes the connection explicit and direct, not a denial.

options.text: He applies it only to future events at the final judgment.
options.note: Paul's application concerns Israel's actual wilderness experience as a type fulfilled already in Christ, not solely a future event.

options.text: He uses it to argue for a different, non-messianic reading of the exodus.
options.note: Paul's reading is explicitly messianic, identifying the rock directly with Christ.

questions: This psalm recalls God's overwhelming presence at the exodus, so overwhelming that sea and mountains seemed to move. Where in your own life have you sensed God's presence powerfully enough to change how you saw a difficult circumstance?
The psalm calls the whole earth to tremble at God's presence. Is your own posture toward God more casual familiarity or reverent awe right now, and what would help restore appropriate trembling?

God turned the hardest flint into a flowing fountain for His thirsty people. What situation in your life currently feels as unyielding as flint, and how does this psalm encourage you to trust God's power to provide from it?
Paul identifies the wilderness rock as a type of Christ, the source of living water. Where are you currently seeking to satisfy a spiritual thirst with something other than Christ, the true Rock?
This psalm retells old history to shape present reverence and trust. What has God done in your past that you need to retell to yourself today to strengthen your faith for a current challenge?

translationNotes.note: Sanctuary renders miqdash, God's holy dwelling place, indicating that the exodus created not merely a free nation but a people among whom God Himself would personally dwell.

The sea, the Jordan, the mountains, and the hills are personified as fleeing, turning back, and skipping, vivid Hebrew poetic devices recalling the Red Sea and Jordan crossings as responses to God's overwhelming presence.
Flint renders challamish, an especially hard and unyielding stone, emphasizing that God's provision of water came from the most improbable and resistant of sources.
